How source-chain assets could support pDAI demand on
PulseChain
A conditional mechanism report, with a PLS-denominated price objective
29 September 2026. Theoretical synthesis based on historical contract models and a read-only
PulseChain audit. The full evidence audit (Appendix 32) is maintained separately, with transaction
references, addresses and reproduction records. No transactions, deployments or governance changes
were made for this report. The numerical examples are mathematical models, not blockchain
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 202

simulations. Deployment observations refer to PulseChain chain 369, block 27,659,393 (28 September
2026), hash 0xc5e582cd902f4bff3b1aa325b9b564fcd5d6dc0ffa77a03fcd105b65c6390275. They are not claims about
every later state. A two-round skeptical review (Appendix 59) separates the surviving conditional result
from stronger claims the report does not prove. The subsequent twelve-point follow-up (Appendix 72)
adds local-exit evidence and bounded financial models, and identifies the unfinished detailed permission
review separately from completed findings.
Abstract
There are coherent conditional paths by which source-chain assets could support purchases
of existing pDAI on PulseChain. A transferable receipt for invested source assets can be locked on its
source chain while an authorized representation circulates on PulseChain. That representation can
support buying power through a market sale, an eligible collateralized issuer, or a funded loan. Other
paths use source-token burning and destination minting, temporary Aave Portal issuance, or Across
delivery funded by existing destination liquidity. These paths have different backing and settlement
requirements, but can converge on purchases of pDAI through local markets.
This report examines possibility rather than requiring an observed end-to-end operation. It treats source-
network operation, specified administrative control and necessary integrations as explicit scenario
assumptions. The audit supplies concrete examples of destination issuance, escrow withdrawals,
governance activity, wrapper acceptance and trading. It does not establish any participant's future plan.
The report makes no attribution of motives or human wallet ownership.
The target is a PulseChain exchange price at which pDAI purchases $1 worth of PLS, using a
stated PLS dollar reference and trade size. Ethereum redemption is not a requirement. A finite-input
market example demonstrates that this target is mathematically reachable in a specified market.
Whether the proposed funding paths can supply the required buying power in actual markets remains a
condition, not a forecast. Reaching the target and maintaining it are separate propositions.
The holder's exit is a local exchange of pDAI for PLS on PulseChain. No bridge to Ethereum or
external-dollar redemption forms part of that outcome. A fee-inclusive extension now demonstrates
thirty successive target-valued local exits under an explicitly funded, bounded scenario, alongside cases
where a smaller budget or changed PLS reference fails. Those are conditional mathematical results
rather than measurements of the deployed network.
The report establishes three limited results: historical mechanisms exist; a stipulated receipt-sale ledger
can finance a purchase without double-counting assets; and sufficient input can reach the target in a
specified market model. It does not derive that funding from validator control or nominal copied
balances. A complete route using the named deployed contracts at the audited snapshot remains
unestablished. The broader claim that control and copied collateral alone ensure the target does not
follow from the conditional result.
1. Define the outcome before discussing the machinery
Let s(t) be the chosen dollar reference for one PLS at time t. Let O(q,t) be the net PLS obtained by selling
q pDAI through the specified PulseChain market route, after its trading fees and price impact. Then:
pDAI execution value(q,t) = s(t) × O(q,t) / q.
The proposed target is an execution value of at least one dollar for the stated quantity. PLS may be
exchanged through its one-for-one wrapped form where the route supports wrapping and unwrapping.
Network costs should be reported separately if the objective is proceeds after all transaction costs.

Thus a compatible local route can end in any of these forms, normalized into PLS units before conversion
costs. Their token addresses remain distinct, and an arbitrary bridged external-ETH token using the
WETH label is not covered by this result. Wrapped claims and the native currency backing them are the
same allocation of assets, not independent reserves that can be added together.
This definition needs a disclosed PLS dollar reference independent of the pDAI market being evaluated,
but does not require pDAI redemption on Ethereum. A copied USDC symbol or an oracle value of one is
not automatically that reference. A marginal pool price, an executable quote for 1,000 pDAI, and the
proceeds from selling billions of pDAI are different measurements. A report claiming the target should
identify which it means.
Because PLS itself has a variable dollar price, a fixed pDAI/PLS ratio does not necessarily maintain a fixed
dollar value. The necessary target ratio changes with s(t). Applying a reference price to a PLS quantity is
a valuation convention. It does not establish that the entire PLS output could be exchanged for that
many external dollars. Any claim of external liquidation proceeds would additionally need the reference
venue's executable depth; that is outside this local target.

2. The premises of the theoretical system
The conditional system considered here assumes:
An operating source environment, such as the proposed pARB, with the stated usable asset balances
and functioning source applications.
Effective authority over the particular bridge, messaging and application roles required by the
selected path. Common administration is a scenario premise, not a conclusion about the identified
wallets.
An authorized destination token integration and, where needed, a compatible collateral adapter,
issuer, lender or market.
Actual destination purchasing liquidity, including the relevant pool outputs or a funded counterparty.
Nominal token quantities are not substituted for executable purchasing power.
Consistent accounting for backing, outstanding claims, fees and settlement.
Copying Ethereum's L1 state did not itself copy every L2 execution database. The source environment is
therefore an additional premise. For theoretical analysis, the absence of a public pARB RPC does not
prevent evaluating that premise; it limits the historical claims that can be made about it.
Validator and messenger authority governs acceptance of cross-chain statements. T oken issuer
permissions govern destination issuance. Application governance governs eligible assets and protocol
settings. These are distinct roles, even when the scenario assigns them to one group. An accepted
statement alone is not an asset with market value. The scenario needs an executable funded exchange
or another explicit funding basis, not merely an asserted balance. A funded pool or lender can
mechanically accept a weakly backed claim and release existing assets. Independent collateral value is
not a universal technical prerequisite for that finite transaction. Its effect on solvency and later
redemptions must be considered separately.
Authority over upgradeable components allows analysis of additional supported configurations. Such
configurations are identified as assumptions rather than inherited capabilities already in operation.
Immutable contracts and unrelated token issuer permissions are not made controllable by ownership of
nearby proxies. This keeps the argument more precise than assuming arbitrary new code can do
anything desired.
Three configuration categories should not be conflated: the observed deployed state, existing code
under different authorized parameters, and new integrations or changed implementations. A
path needing a new collateral adapter or token mapping belongs to the third category until its exact
interface is specified. Historical code availability does not by itself put it in the first category. This report
does not use arbitrary replacement code as proof that the inherited infrastructure already supplies a
complete route.
The required control assumption also affects the credibility of claims. An authority able to change source
balances or custody rules may affect dilution and redemption expectations. Control establishes neither a
market haircut nor a guaranteed price; funded acceptance and any assumed constraints on later
changes must be specified separately.
3. The principal path: invested assets become a marketable claim
The central intuition has a coherent accounting form:

In this model the bridge holds the receipt, while its underlying assets can remain invested in the source
protocol. The destination representation is a claim on that receipt. Neither the source underlying nor the
same receipt can also remain independently spendable by the original depositor.
Transferable ERC-20/PRC-20 tokens, transferable ERC-4626 vault shares, cT okens and static lending
receipts are relevant asset forms. Rebasing receipts need compatible share/rate accounting; their
changing balances are not automatically synchronized across chains. Nontransferable positions and NFT
interfaces do not fit an ordinary fungible-token gateway merely by sharing a descriptive label. ERC-4626
itself permits nontransferable shares, and its conversion views are not guarantees of executable
redemption. The actual share transfer and withdrawal rules matter. Its normal asset-funded mint method
is not a general bridge mint permission. ERC-4626 specification.
Three destination choices can turn this representation into purchasing power:
Direct sale. A market accepts the exact representation and exchanges pDAI, PLS or an intermediate
asset for it. The buyer or pool acquires the claim.
Local collateralized issuance. An existing issuer accepts the representation as eligible backing
and creates its own token. A pool already listing that issuer's token can accept it without treating the
bridge representation as the same token.
Funded borrowing. A lender accepts the representation as collateral and lends existing destination
assets. Those assets can fund a purchase, while the borrower retains a repayment obligation.
None of these choices requires Aave Portal. Their common economic requirement is that the delivered
claim obtains actual buying power on PulseChain.
Exact token identity matters
A representation of source aDAI is not automatically the existing PulseChain Aave aDAI contract.
Similarly, a bridged token called eUSD is not automatically the eUSD address already accepted by a
Curve pool. Shared symbols, decimals or numerical addresses across chains do not establish
interchangeability.
The local-issuer route provides a separate way to obtain an existing pool coin: The bridge delivers
collateral X, and the local issuer creates token Y against eligible X. X and Y remain different assets.
Reserve eUSD supplies a concrete basket-based architecture for this distinction. Its collateral
registration, active basket, valuation, issuance limits and actual transfers must all fit the hypothetical
configuration. In a multi-asset basket, supplying one component does not replace the others.
The audit found an existing eUSD issuer and a Curve pool accepting that exact eUSD token. It did not
find a newly installed pARB receipt in the sampled eUSD basket. The additional integration is an explicit
condition of this path. Reserve source and state study (Appendix 18).

What “backed” means in this argument
Custody coverage means the representations correspond to exclusive source receipts. Source
solvency concerns whether those receipts' underlying claims are recoverable against the source
protocol's assets and liabilities. Redemption liquidity concerns what can actually be withdrawn, and
when. Purchasing capacity is the quantity of destination assets that an executable sale or funded loan
delivers. None of these measures alone establishes all the others. A trillion units can be fully escrowed
and receive no funded bid.
A collateral oracle can affect what a configured protocol accepts. It cannot by itself create the output
assets paid by that protocol. Conversely, a protocol can spend its existing inventory against a declared
collateral value even if later liquidation would recover less. The finite purchase can succeed while the
funder bears a shortfall. That distinction is necessary for a neutral assessment of technical possibility
and economic sustainability.

These are different ways to mobilize or relocate assets. A source receipt can remain invested in the sale,
borrowing or issuance examples; in the Across example that remains possible only if the configured
source asset is an admissible investment receipt. The same source allocation cannot remain freely
spendable by the original holder after being sold, pledged or used as backing.
For example, a funded lender can advance 700 PLS against an accepted 100-unit representation.
Spending those 700 PLS creates a local purchase while leaving a 700-PLS principal debt. Its future
payment does not have to occur before the purchase, but belongs in the support horizon when due.
Another example issues 100 local issuer tokens against eligible collateral and sells them for 700 PLS; the
output market supplies those PLS and inherits the issued claim. These are stipulated quantities, not
dollar valuations or observed offers.
For Portal, issuing 100 pDAI-equivalent claims and selling their wrapper for 99.9 pDAI can be fully settled
with a separately funded 0.1-pDAI contribution when the backing fee is zero. The operator then holds no
free pDAI from that cycle; the market holds claims and Aave holds 100 pDAI backing them. This closes
the accounting instead of leaving the shortfall implicit. Each stage must also pass its own post-operation
deposit limits and other validation conditions.
These financing parties may have later settlement or redemption obligations. The pDAI holder's local
PLS exit does not require performing those obligations or bridging out. They matter to how
much funding remains available and whether the financing system can repeat its operations.

Arbitrum reverse gateways: the receipt can stay invested
The historical reverse-gateway model locks native source tokens and mints their authorized L1
representation. For a transferable vault receipt, this preserves source investment while changing who
can circulate the claim. In a simple one-to-one, non-rebasing model, outstanding representations must
correspond to the receipts committed to them. The same escrow allocation cannot independently back
multiple unrestricted claims.
At settled checkpoints, representation supply can equal its allocated escrow. During asynchronous
transfers, account for exclusive pending issuance and return rights as well. In a simple lossless model
without donations, rebasing, fees or other allocations:
committed escrow = outstanding representations + pending issuance rights + pending return rights.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 209

Each right is counted once as it changes status; this is an accounting model, not a claim that every term
is exposed by an existing getter. Multiple destinations must be reconciled against the same allocation. If
its holder chooses a source return, the representation is retired before the corresponding source receipt
is released. This is not a prerequisite for a pDAI holder's local PLS exit. The receipt holder can then seek
source redemption under that vault's limits, queues and solvency. The receipt's current asset conversion
rate is separate from its bridged share count; a destination oracle does not automatically track or
enforce that rate.
Historical reverse-gateway code and ARB's inherited integration demonstrate the architecture. The
recorded PulseChain ARB transaction demonstrates destination minting. Applying the architecture to a
different receipt still requires that receipt's own integration and destination acceptance. Historical source
and accounting (Appendix 13).
GRT and LPT: token-specific issuance can replace missing escrow
GRT is the clearest executed example of a destination escrow shortfall being filled by issuance. The
September 2026 transaction combined 1 existing GRT with 62,875,936.675361278837595998 newly
minted GRT. Its mint authority and allowance parameters were inherited; the allowance accumulated
with block height.
The historical GRT model burns withdrawn source GRT and can mint an allowed shortfall on L1. It
therefore supports a distinct part of the thesis: sufficient pre-existing L1 escrow is not universally
necessary for delivery of an integrated token. It does not demonstrate continued investment of the same
withdrawn GRT. Official historical GIP-0037, PulseChain transaction reconciliation (Appendix 12).
LPT's gateway source includes an external-minter shortfall branch, but the recorded LPT withdrawal used
existing escrow. HGOLD's gateway contains a bridge-mint call, while current token-level permission
remains unresolved and the selected post-fork search found no execution. These are additional
capability categories, not additional demonstrated mint transactions. Specialized gateway study
(Appendix 20).
Aave Portal: temporary local issuance with a backing obligation
Portal can create the ordinary destination aT oken before destination underlying arrives, subject to bridge
authorization and reserve checks. A compatible static wrapper can accept that aT oken, and a market
accepting the exact wrapper may exchange existing pDAI for it. This can move pDAI from an AMM into
Aave's backing flow while leaving the market holding wrapper shares whose underlying redemption
remains subject to Aave cash and withdrawal rules.
Portal has an additional accounting obligation: the destination reserve's unbacked amount must be
settled with its actual underlying asset. Source collateral can support the funder's obligation, but it does
not itself become cash inside destination Aave. Ordinary supply and ordinary loan repayment do not
settle Portal's unbacked balance.
For a DAI-reserve Portal cycle, if M units of pDAI principal produce Q pDAI from selling the compatible
wrapper, backing principal plus an actual backing fee F solely from those proceeds requires Q >= M + F. A
shortfall requires separate funding. After backing, the transferred pDAI is reserve cash supporting
outstanding claims; it is not also free treasury inventory. Backing USDC or USDT issuance requires that
reserve's underlying, not simply the DAI obtained from a different sale.
This path can affect liquidity distribution and trading prices. It is not, by itself, an unlimited source of net
assets or permanently locked pDAI. The audited stablecoin Portal caps were zero, so enabled operation is
an additional scenario condition rather than an observed configuration. There is also an independent
supply-cap barrier: sampled DAI aT oken supply was about 398.79 million against a 338 million cap,
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 210

and USDT supply about 720.91 million against a 200 million cap. The deployed Portal path applies
supply validation as well as the unbacked cap. Enabling Portal capacity alone would not establish those
paths' availability under otherwise unchanged state. Deployed-code accounting and wrapper study
(Appendix 17).
Across: financing delivery through existing destination capital
Across can connect source capital to an L1 purchase without requiring the same units to complete a
canonical bridge transfer first. A source deposit supports a relayer delivering existing PulseChain tokens.
The recipient may then trade or supply those tokens locally, while later settlement repays the relayer.
If repayment occurs on the source chain, assets can remain on that network while the relayer's inventory
changes location. The same source deposit does not remain an unrestricted claim of the original
depositor after repayment. Source spoke replenishment, destination hub replenishment and relayer
inventory are separate balances.
Supported callbacks can combine destination delivery with a local DeFi action. That local transaction can
be atomic; the entire cross-chain sequence is not. Continuous one-direction delivery needs replenished
destination capital, offsetting flows or another funded credit arrangement. The current copied spoke's
replacement implementation was not source-verified in the audit, so its inherited callback behavior is not
assumed unchanged. Historical Across model and balance example (Appendix 7), actual HubPool/spoke
observations (Appendix 14).
Gnosis, Polygon and ordinary return bridges
Gnosis Omnibridge's historical reverse mode supports source-native custody and destination
representations, including representation creation through its factory model. This can accommodate a
transferable source receipt in a compatible integration. Gnosis is a separate chain, not an Arbitrum
rollup. The separate xDAI bridge's DAI-origin return releases its backing and is not the generic
Omnibridge reverse-mint mechanism.
Polygon PoS's historical mintable predicate supplies a different source-burn / root-mint model. It can use
root inventory and mint a shortfall when authorized for that root token. Ordinary escrow predicates do
not acquire that permission merely by sharing Polygon's messaging infrastructure.
The audit established inherited PulseChain-side presence for an Omnibridge proxy and a Polygon
mintable-predicate proxy. It did not establish every operational counterpart or token mapping; the
sampled Polygon implementation also lacked verified explorer source. Their conditional roles are
anchored in historical code, with deployment-specific behavior left as an assumption. Historical sources
and presence reads (Appendix 7).
Ordinary Arbitrum and legacy Optimism returns remain useful when destination escrow is funded. They
provide existing assets, not a general shortfall-mint facility. Their contribution is transport of available
purchasing assets.
Other protocol families and downstream liquidity
Reserve issuance and receipt-backed borrowing are destination uses of collateral, not separate bridge
types. Origin, mStable and other issuers have their own supported assets and valuation rules; lending
systems, including different Aave or Morpho designs, have their own eligibility and funding rules. The
report does not assign those names generic acceptance of an arbitrary pARB receipt. No new Origin/
Morpho-specific collateral route is established by this synthesis.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 211

FRAX AMO issuance or lending can contribute FRAX where their own conditions permit it. Ferry transports
balances. Supplying FRAX to one pool does not itself replace USDC, DAI or PLS paid out by the next pool.
Similarly, a stkAAVE upgrade does not by itself establish an operating GHO issuer; the sampled GHO
linkage was not operationally established. These may be additional integrations in a scenario, rather
than presumed sources of unlimited cash.
Authenticated messengers and AMBs can connect compatible applications, but the destination receiver
determines whether a message transfers, mints or records something. A message is not itself a token or
purchasing asset. New custom systems are possible in principle, but cannot be catalogued as already
inherited protocol capabilities without specifying their accounting and authorization.
5. How the paths converge on pDAI demand
Once a participant has an accepted destination asset, an available route might exchange it directly for
pDAI or pass through FRAX and USDC first. The eUSD/FRAXBP, FRAX/base-pool and other Curve
connections supply possible market links; actual mUSD-to-DAI exchanges and Aave-wrapper trades
supply observations of individual local links. This supports the composition argument without claiming
the bridge mints financed those observed trades.
Purchases increase the input asset held by the market and decrease its pDAI inventory. AMM prices
respond to the resulting balances. An acquired pDAI can be retained, supplied, escrowed or used to
settle an obligation, but those choices have different effects on later availability. Aave deposits and
bridge escrow are commitments with release conditions, not necessarily permanent burns.
Finite output liquidity remains relevant even when mint capacity is large. A pool limit can mean available
cash, a pricing constraint, an issuance cap, or a replenishing rate limit. These are not interchangeable.
Adding appropriate liquidity may increase capacity, but also changes inventory and the price path;
adding more of the token being sold does not conjure the missing output asset. Balancer limits and
observed swaps (Appendix 16).
The circulating supply need not all be purchased to raise a market price. Conversely, a numerical
issuance ceiling larger than total pDAI supply does not prove sufficient buying power. A receipt's
conversion rate, market discount, fees, competing pools and newly offered pDAI determine the relevant

7. From reaching a price to sustaining it
For a specified market state and seller-flow scenario, let C be the actual input assets required to reach
the target and B the purchasing assets available from all selected financing paths, after immediate costs
and reserved settlement funding. Express B and C in the same spendable input asset after required
conversions, including conversion fees and price impact; do not add face values of different claims. A
funded route with B >= C can support that modeled intervention if all intervening contract operations are
executable. This is a conditional sufficiency statement, not a measured inequality for the audited
network.
The sequence must also be funded at every intermediate step, in each required asset. A positive final
balance does not finance an earlier payment. This is a cash-feasibility condition, distinct from the
economic solvency of collateral. Cross-chain settlement delays cannot be treated as a single atomic
transaction. Route budgets sharing collateral, lender cash, relayer inventory or base-pool liquidity cannot
be added independently. Quotes must reflect the state left by preceding trades, not mutually
incompatible uses of the same initial balances.
Do not subtract every long-term loan principal as if it were payable immediately: credit can finance a
current purchase while its debt remains outstanding. But that liability must remain in the system's
balance sheet. A claim of a repeatable, self-financing process additionally needs resources for eventual
repayment, redemption, fees, losses and reserve replenishment.
Below the target, funded buying can support demand. Above it, selling retained pDAI can add supply and
rebuild reserves. This feedback policy can be described without assuming a particular operator has
adopted it. It does not guarantee a durable peg: selling pressure can exceed the available intervention
budget, and the assets backing that budget can change value.
A bounded support claim needs a disclosed time horizon, execution quantity, permitted price band,
seller and redemption flows, available purchasing inventory, debt maturities, and replenishment
assumptions. An above-target sale also requires available pDAI inventory. Fees, realized income, new
contributed capital or profitable trades may replenish reserves; merely specifying a buy/sell rule does
not establish those inflows. No finite budget guarantees the target under arbitrary unbounded selling
pressure.

Abstract
There are coherent conditional paths by which source-chain assets could support purchases
of existing pDAI on PulseChain. A transferable receipt for invested source assets can be locked on its
source chain while an authorized representation circulates on PulseChain. That representation can
support buying power through a market sale, an eligible collateralized issuer, or a funded loan. Other
paths use source-token burning and destination minting, temporary Aave Portal issuance, or Across
delivery funded by existing destination liquidity. These paths have different backing and settlement
requirements, but can converge on purchases of pDAI through local markets.
This report examines possibility rather than requiring an observed end-to-end operation. It treats source-
network operation, specified administrative control and necessary integrations as explicit scenario
assumptions. The audit supplies concrete examples of destination issuance, escrow withdrawals,
governance activity, wrapper acceptance and trading. It does not establish any participant's future plan.
The report makes no attribution of motives or human wallet ownership.
The target is a PulseChain exchange price at which pDAI purchases $1 worth of PLS, using a
stated PLS dollar reference and trade size. Ethereum redemption is not a requirement. A finite-input
market example demonstrates that this target is mathematically reachable in a specified market.
Whether the proposed funding paths can supply the required buying power in actual markets remains a
condition, not a forecast. Reaching the target and maintaining it are separate propositions.
The holder's exit is a local exchange of pDAI for PLS on PulseChain. No bridge to Ethereum or
external-dollar redemption forms part of that outcome. A fee-inclusive extension now demonstrates
thirty successive target-valued local exits under an explicitly funded, bounded scenario, alongside cases
where a smaller budget or changed PLS reference fails. Those are conditional mathematical results
rather than measurements of the deployed network.
The report establishes three limited results: historical mechanisms exist; a stipulated receipt-sale ledger
can finance a purchase without double-counting assets; and sufficient input can reach the target in a
specified market model. It does not derive that funding from validator control or nominal copied
balances. A complete route using the named deployed contracts at the audited snapshot remains
unestablished. The broader claim that control and copied collateral alone ensure the target does not
follow from the conditional result.

2. The premises of the theoretical system
The conditional system considered here assumes:
An operating source environment, such as the proposed pARB, with the stated usable asset balances
and functioning source applications.
Effective authority over the particular bridge, messaging and application roles required by the
selected path. Common administration is a scenario premise, not a conclusion about the identified
wallets.
An authorized destination token integration and, where needed, a compatible collateral adapter,
issuer, lender or market.
Actual destination purchasing liquidity, including the relevant pool outputs or a funded counterparty.
Nominal token quantities are not substituted for executable purchasing power.
Consistent accounting for backing, outstanding claims, fees and settlement.
Copying Ethereum's L1 state did not itself copy every L2 execution database. The source environment is
therefore an additional premise. For theoretical analysis, the absence of a public pARB RPC does not
prevent evaluating that premise; it limits the historical claims that can be made about it.
Validator and messenger authority governs acceptance of cross-chain statements. T oken issuer
permissions govern destination issuance. Application governance governs eligible assets and protocol
settings. These are distinct roles, even when the scenario assigns them to one group. An accepted
statement alone is not an asset with market value. The scenario needs an executable funded exchange
or another explicit funding basis, not merely an asserted balance. A funded pool or lender can
mechanically accept a weakly backed claim and release existing assets. Independent collateral value is
not a universal technical prerequisite for that finite transaction. Its effect on solvency and later
redemptions must be considered separately.
Authority over upgradeable components allows analysis of additional supported configurations. Such
configurations are identified as assumptions rather than inherited capabilities already in operation.
Immutable contracts and unrelated token issuer permissions are not made controllable by ownership of

rebuild reserves. This feedback policy can be described without assuming a particular operator has

If authority extends to the exact token issuer, authorized issuance may also increase the spendable
units of that token. It would therefore be too strong to say governance can never add token balances.
However, changing a lender's limits or oracle marks alone does not create an unrelated output asset.
Issuing more units does not guarantee the executable PLS value required for the target. Application
governance also does not imply control of native PLS issuance or consensus rules; that would be a
different system assumption.
Governance feasibility includes the required voting power, quorum, proposal and execution permissions,
timelocks, implementation bounds and successful execution. A declared common owner does not
substitute for all those conditions. The existing control evidence is narrower: Aave V2 changes do not
prove V3 ACL control; a stkAAVE upgrade does not establish GHO; Across changes do not establish
control of all UMA dependencies; and the Reserve role studies do not establish the named group's
effective voting control. These are evidence limits, not contradictions of the explicit common-control
assumption in this theoretical exercise.
Consequently, the present-state barriers should be read as requirements to resolve, not permanent
disproofs. A successfully reconfigured and funded system could support a finite purchase. Whether it can
repeat the operation solvently and defend the target remains a separate balance-sheet and market
question. Governance is a potentially important enabling mechanism within the theory, not a substitute
for that analysis.

The narrowed conditional mechanism is coherent. Source receipts can preserve invested assets
while an authorized destination claim is monetized; specialized token issuance, temporary protocol
credit and funded bridge delivery provide additional paths. Their outputs can converge on purchases of
pDAI. A sufficiently funded market intervention can reach a stated PLS-valued target in a specified
market, as the finite-input example demonstrates.

The extended model supports a bounded sequence of fee-paying local exits and an inventory-
constrained sell-above-target example under assumed PLS appreciation. Native PLS, canonical WPLS and
the exact inherited WETH contract can be evaluated through their native-unit conversion paths. None of
these local outcomes requires the pDAI holder to bridge to Ethereum. Appreciation is an explicit
scenario; its occurrence as a consequence of the peg is not established by the model.
The stipulated financing ledger shows where purchasing assets come from and where each claim ends
up. It does not show that nominal copied collateral or validator control generates those assets. Funded
mechanical acceptance can permit a finite purchase even when collateral is economically weak; that fact
does not establish solvent repetition or a durable peg.
The report therefore supports conditional architectural possibility and a specified market-level existence
example. It does not establish a complete route executable in the audited deployed configuration, that
the named wallets adopted this mechanism as their plan, or that pDAI will reach or maintain the target.
Those stronger conclusions require the additional proof obligations above.
